Issued at 126 AM CDT Thu Sep 10 2026

A small upper-level ridge will be moving over SD today which helps 
to push a high pressure out of the state. The southerly flow along 
the backside of the high pressure will push warm, dry air into SD. 
The warm air moving in will help to warm temperatures today and 
Friday about 5-15 degrees warmer than normal, with highs in the low 
80s to low 90s. The drier air moving in will lower the humidity over 
central and northeastern SD, with areas west of the Missouri River 
seeing the humidity drop down between 15-25 percent. This dryness 
along with the dry fuels in areas west of the Missouri River is 
leading to elevated fire concerns. One of the things lowering the 
concern is that winds will be fairly marginal, with low chances of 
the winds gusting up to 25 mph this afternoon when and where the 
humidity is the lowest. There is still high grassland fire danger 
index values over some of the areas west of the Missouri River 
because the dryness will make it fairly easy for something to 
ignite. 

A low level jet will be developing tonight into Friday over eastern 
SD. This jet will be helping to move more moisture and warm air into 
northeastern SD Friday as well as strengthen the winds at the 
surface over this area, with a 30-60% chance for winds to gust more 
than 35 mph early Friday morning, especially along the eastern edge 
of the Prairie Coteau (over I-29). A surface low, as well as warm 
front and dryline, will be moving over SD Friday morning and will 
sit there through most of the day before a cold front comes in 
Friday evening to push everything to the southeast. Since 
northeastern SD will be in the warm sector of this low, the warm, 
moist air will continue moving into the area, helping to increase 
the instability. The NAM has CAPE values getting up between 1000-
3000 J/kg over northeastern SD Friday afternoon. This will help 
storms to develop as the cold front moves through late Friday 
afternoon into the evening. Right now, the models vary how fast the 
front moves through, with some models moving it through quicker and 
keeping the chance for storms to develop out of northeastern SD, 
while other models are a bit slower and have storms developing more 
in northeastern SD and sticking around for a bit longer. There is a 
slight (level 2 of 5) to marginal (level 1 of 5) risk for these 
storms to become severe. The model soundings over northeastern SD 
have some drier mid-level air with steep lapse rates of 7-8 C/km. 
This will help to drive a strong wind threat in the storms if they 
do develop over the area, with gusts of 60-75 mph possible due to 
the potential for a microburst or two. Additionally, since the 
storms that develop could be elevated with the strong lapse rates, 
there could be hail up to 2 inches that falls from the storms. The 
model sounding's hodographs show some directional low level shear 
that could cause some turning in the storms. While the storms do 
appear to be elevated in nature, if a storm or two were to develop 
closer to the ground, the development of a tornado or two cannot be 
ruled out.

Behind the dry line moving in Friday with the weak surface low, 
relative humidities will drop down again, with values of 15-25% 
possible over portions of south central SD. As the cold front moves 
in Friday afternoon, the wind speeds behind it will pick up and will 
start to affect the areas with lower humidity values. Wind speeds 
over central SD will be able to gust up around 30-40 mph Friday 
afternoon into the evening. This creates even higher fire weather 
concerns than today, especially over portions of south central SD. 
With the winds, low humidity, and dry fuels, there is high to very 
high grassland fire danger index values. An eye will need to be kept 
on the mixing potential needed to get the strong winds to the 
surface as well as the fire weather concerns as the components are 
there for a Red Flag Warning. If a fire were to ignite, it would 
become difficult to suppress or control, and with the shifting winds 
from the frontal passage it could cause changes in fire behavior if 
something were to be burning. 

High surface pressure will be moving in behind the cold front as 
well some cooler temperatures. The temperatures over central and 
northeastern SD and west central MN will be slightly below normal, 
with highs this weekend in the 60s to low 70s. The high pressure 
will help to keep showers and storms from developing Saturday. 
Models are forecasting another frontal boundary moving through Sunday 
into Monday, which will likely cause showers and storms to occur 
over central and northeastern SD, though models do vary the 
starting time of the showers and storms.
